analysis.headline: Passed the House 231-199 (Roll no. 496) on July 18, 2019; the Senate placed it on its Legislative Calendar under General Orders and it never received a Senate vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Raise the Wage Act would have raised the federal minimum wage in annual steps from $8.40 to $15.00 over six years, and after that adjusted it each year to keep pace with the growth in the median hourly wage [S5]. It would also have phased out the lower minimum wages allowed for tipped workers, for newly hired workers under 20, and for workers with disabilities, so that each group would eventually be paid the same minimum wage as everyone else [S2][S4]. The bill passed the House but never came up for a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid near the federal minimum wage, including tipped workers whose cash wage was as low as $2.13 an hour under prior law, newly hired teenagers, and workers with disabilities paid under special subminimum-wage certificates. All would eventually move to the full minimum wage [S2][S4][S5].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in annual steps — $8.40 first, then $9.50, $10.60, $11.70, $12.80, $13.90, and $15.00 six years after the effective date [S5].

After reaching $15.00, the minimum wage would rise each year by the percentage increase in the median hourly wage of all employees, as measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, so it would not erode with inflation [S5].

It eliminates the separate, lower minimum wage for tipped employees, phasing their cash wage up by $1.50 a year until it equals the full minimum wage, and gives employees the right to retain their tips [S5].

It phases out the subminimum wage for workers with disabilities by raising the special certificate wage each year until it equals the full minimum wage, bars any new special certificates, and directs the Department of Labor to provide transition assistance and help ensure continuing employment opportunities for affected workers [S4][S2].
It phases out the separate $4.25 training wage for newly hired workers under 20, stepping it up until it equals the full minimum wage [S5][S4].

It requires the Department of Labor to publish each increase 60 days before it takes effect, and requires Government Accountability Office reports on the impact of the first two increases on businesses, including small businesses, with Congress directed to assess the findings and consider actions such as delaying later increases [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage labor — restaurants, retail, agriculture, and other businesses that rely on minimum-wage workers, including employers who used the tipped-employee cash wage and holders of subminimum-wage certificates for workers with disabilities — would pay materially higher hourly wages, and employers using the 14(c) special certificates would lose the ability to pay below the minimum wage [S2][S4][S5].

drawbacks.text: Opponents in the House sought to exempt very small firms from the increase: the Republican motion to recommit would have sent the bill back with an amendment titled 'Small Business Survival' exempting enterprises that employ fewer than 10 individuals with annual gross sales under $1,000,000; it failed 210-218, with 195 of 199 voting Republicans in favor [S7][S8].

The bill itself acknowledges a transition risk for workers with disabilities: it directs the Department of Labor to help employers 'ensur[e] continuing employment opportunities' for people now paid under special subminimum certificates, implying that ending those certificates could jeopardize some of those jobs [S2][S4].

The bill anticipated business effects and built in monitoring rather than exemptions: it requires a GAO report on how the first two increases affect businesses' employment, prices, revenues, turnover, and hiring and training costs, with Congress instructed to assess the findings and consider actions including delaying the next scheduled increases [S4][S5].

The phase-in is gradual — the first step is only to $8.40, and $15.00 is not reached until six years after enactment — so the immediate benefit at enactment is modest for workers already earning above that [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a direct pay raise to minimum-wage and tipped workers nationwide and end long-standing subminimum wage tiers, with the cost falling on the businesses that employ them, likely passed on partly through prices and adjusted schedules. The strongest good-faith objections are about small-business and regional impacts and about employment for workers with disabilities losing their special certificates; the bill addressed the first with multi-year phase-ins, notice requirements, GAO studies, and a congressional review mechanism that could delay later increases, and addressed the second with transition assistance, but did not exempt small firms from the mandate.

outcome.mechanism: Passed the House 231-199, then was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 156), where it remained with no further action through the end of the 116th Congress.

narrative.text: Introduced January 16, 2019 by Rep. Bobby Scott and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S7][S1].
The committee held a markup on March 6, 2019 and ordered the bill reported in the nature of a substitute by a 28-20 vote; it was reported amended on July 11, 2019 (H. Rept. 116-150) [S7].

The House considered the bill under a rule (H. Res. 492) on July 18, 2019; a motion to recommit with instructions to add a small-business exemption failed 210-218 (Roll no. 495), and the bill passed 231-199 (Roll no. 496), with 228 of 234 voting Democrats in favor and 3 of 195 voting Republicans in favor [S7][S8][S9].

The Senate received the bill on July 18, 2019, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 156 on July 22, 2019; no further action was taken before the Congress ended [S7][S5].

key_actors.name: Robert C. "Bobby" Scott
key_actors.role: U.S. Representative (D-VA); bill sponsor and Chairman of the House Committee on Education and Labor
key_actors.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill; his committee held a markup on March 6, 2019 that ordered the bill reported 28-20, and reported it amended on July 11, 2019 [S7][S1].

key_actors.name: House Education and Labor Committee
key_actors.what_they_did: Reported the bill amended by a 28-20 vote, moving it to the House floor [S7].

key_actors.name: U.S. Senate (116th Congress)
key_actors.role: Chamber that received the bill after House passage
key_actors.what_they_did: Received the bill, read it twice, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 22, 2019; no debate, amendment, or vote ever occurred, and the Congress ended January 3, 2021 with the bill still on the calendar [S7][S5].
